claims.text: By the end of episode 7, Rhaena was separated from a wounded Sheepstealer, Alicent had poisoned Aemond, Ulf had secretly agreed to defect to Ormund, Sunfyre had returned to Aegon, Rhaenyra and Mysaria had become intimate, and Helaena's vision had shown Dreamfyre.
Episode 7 established Sunfyre's return and reunion with Aegon, showed Dreamfyre within Helaena's vision, and established Ormund winning Ulf's secret cooperation.
Criticism of episode 7 focused on its brooding, vision-heavy structure and on frustration with characters repeating psychological loops while the war advanced elsewhere.
Audience reaction after episode 7 was notably protective of Sheepstealer after the dragon was wounded, separated from Rhaena, and left with an uncertain fate.
Episode 6 killed Criston Cole at the Butcher's Ball, advanced the northern and river forces toward Tumbleton, and ended with Corlys captive as the ground war converged on the finale.
Episode 5 continued Aegon and Larys's road story, revealed Helaena's pregnancy, and made Alicent and Helaena's attempt to escape a consequential late-season thread.
Episode 3 established Rhaenyra's governance and resource problems in King's Landing, including missing royal funds, shortages, and the Red Keep's rat infestation.
Alive but has ABANDONED Aegon and Tyland rather than face the confrontation. Destination not established.
ENJOYED. The Aegon/Larys/Tyland road story is a strong approval area, and Larys finally snapping at Aegon was called 'so damn satisfying'.

Alive and SECRETLY TURNED TO THE GREENS in E7, won over by Ormund with respect, pleasure and the promise of Driftmark. CRITICALLY: nobody on Team Black knows. Rhaenyra and Daemon still count him and Silverwing as theirs. The audience knows; the characters do not.

SURPRISINGLY WELL LIKED. Obnoxious, but the show made his resentment comprehensible — 'Ulf's motives are completely understandable' is a common note. Viewers condemn the behaviour while buying the psychology.
Alive, at Harrenhal, having just poisoned Aemond as the price of Rhaenyra protecting Helaena.

THE WRITING IS THE TARGET, NOT THE ACTOR. The poisoning is the focal point of a 'they broke Alicent' argument. Crucially, viewers are sympathetic to Olivia Cooke and think she is excellent — they are unhappy with what the scripts ask her to sell. Do not mock the performance.
Alive and STILL BLACK-ALIGNED on screen. Tied to occupied Tumbleton through his wife Kat, who refuses to leave with him. Loyalty strained — but no defection has happened.
UNDER-DISCUSSED relative to Ulf. A suspense character rather than a fandom character — the conversation is about Kat, the dragonseeds and what he will choose, rather than about him.
Alive at Harrenhal, standing over the poisoned Aemond, and in possession of a hidden clutch of dragon eggs.
DIVISIVE BUT COMPELLING. Rankin's uncanny performance is praised; the Aemond material splits between enthusiasm and Harrenhal fatigue.
Alive, commanding the Winter Wolves, closing on the Hightower position at Tumbleton.
WELL LIKED. The dry, brutal veteran is a popular addition.
Alive, revealed to have survived the Gullet, and staying with Aegon after volunteering to stand beside him.
ENJOYED as part of the Aegon/Larys/Tyland trio.
Alive, severely scarred, returned in E7 and killed the Black soldiers confronting Aegon. The show does not explain how he survived.

ENORMOUSLY POPULAR. His return is the crowd-pleaser of the season — 'Sunfyre really saved the episode'. Viewers respond to the mirroring: scarred king, scarred dragon, both wrecked by the same war. Aegon calling him 'his boy' is widely quoted.
Alive at Tumbleton, increasingly opposed to Ormund and protective of Daeron. Exposed a fake Baratheon assassination attempt.
LIKED as the Green side's conscience.
Alive in King's Landing as Rhaenyra's spymaster and intimate partner.

ONE OF THE CLEAREST AUDIENCE LOSERS — but the complaint is screen time, not the character. 'The fact Mysaria gets more scenes than Aegon is criminal.' The argument is that the Rhaenyra/Mysaria material crowds out the war, Aegon and the dragons. Some viewers do like the chemistry.
Alive and an active Black dragonrider; helped contain Sheepstealer and escort the queen’s retreat.
QUIETLY LIKED. His loyalty reads well against Rhaenyra's mistrust of the dragonseeds.
Alive at Tumbleton. Used in the killing of Kat's brother Leo.
Well liked. Viewers respond to Daeron calling her 'his girl' — read as a genuine bond, set against Ormund's purely instrumental view of dragons.
Alive. Goes with Ulf to the Greens after his secret defection — Team Black does not know.
Discussed mostly as the asset Ulf is taking with him.
Alive. WHEREABOUTS UNKNOWN — deliberately left unclear since E5. Do not place her.
Her absence is one of the season's most-discussed open questions.
Alive in occupied Tumbleton, refusing to leave with Hugh.
SYMPATHETIC, though viewers question why she will not leave Tumbleton.
Alive in King's Landing, serving whichever regime holds it.
LOW PROFILE.
Alive; Ormund’s operative, having successfully kidnapped Corlys.
LOW PROFILE.
Alive. Took part in the Sheepstealer fight.
Neutral.
Badly wounded in E7 after fighting Syrax, Seasmoke and Caraxes at once. Daemon deliberately let him escape. Alive, alone, injured.

THE BREAKOUT OF THE SEASON. 'Justice for Sheepstealer' is the dominant meme — viewers treat him as an innocent dragged into Targaryen nonsense who was 'minding his own business taking sheep'. Genuine sadness, not only jokes, about him being set on by three dragons. Widely admired for surviving 3-v-1. He is more sympathetic to the audience than his own rider.
Alive, reconciled with Rhaena, still one of Rhaenyra’s functioning riders.
LIKED. Some find the Alyn romance under-developed; others are glad she has a life beyond being Jace's fiancée.
Alive. The Bronze Fury, one of the largest living dragons — and the reason Hugh matters strategically.
Treated as a looming strategic factor rather than a personality.
Alive, co-commanding the Riverlands force closing on Tumbleton.
POSITIVE but lower profile.
Alive, in King's Landing, holding the Iron Throne after recovering Rhaena. Facing an empty treasury, food shortages, a hostile Faith and restive dragonseeds.

GOODWILL DETERIORATING. The complaint is not that she is evil but that her decisions look self-destructive — alienating dragonseeds, mistrusting advisers, mishandling the city. 'Rhaenyra's downfall' is now a common video title. Viewers are actively arguing whether this is good tragedy or bad writing.
Alive, controls Tumbleton, holds Corlys prisoner, and has secretly turned Ulf. A large Black northern host is closing on him.

LOVE TO HATE. 'I hate this man, give me more of this man.' People hate what he does to Daeron and enjoy watching him do it. Note the difference from Alicent criticism: nobody wants Ormund's scenes removed, they want to analyse them.
Alive as far as E7 establishes. His exact position late in the season is NOT re-established — do not invent a battlefield location for him.
LOW PROFILE.
Alive. Last confirmed at the Sheepstealer fight, having deliberately let the wounded dragon escape. Exact location after that scene is NOT established — do not place him.

DEBATABLE. Viewers were divided on him, but E7 earned real credit: many noticed he could have had Caraxes finish Sheepstealer and deliberately chose not to, reading it as choosing his daughter over the obvious move.
Alive but a PRISONER of Ormund at Tumbleton, missing a finger — sent to Alyn as proof.
SYMPATHETIC, though viewers find it implausible that so experienced a warlord was kidnapped so easily.
Alive, returned to King's Landing with Rhaenyra after her secret was exposed. Sheepstealer is wounded and gone.

POLARIZED — and notably less liked than her dragon. Some credit her finally getting agency; a substantial contingent blames her for dragging Sheepstealer into a war he had no part in. Rule of thumb: Rhaena is a debate, Sheepstealer is applause.
Alive, scarred and disabled, on the road with Tyland, newly re-emboldened after Sunfyre returned and killed the Black soldiers confronting him.

THE SEASON'S BIGGEST WINNER. Viewers who mocked him now name him a favourite. The wounded road story stripped the swagger and made him a person. You do not have to back him politically to enjoy watching him.
Alive. Fought Sheepstealer in E7; Daemon chose not to finish him.
Respected. The choice not to kill Sheepstealer earned Daemon credit.
Alive at Tumbleton, resisting Ormund’s attempts to make him a puppet king, with Gwayne acting as a counterweight.

A SUCCESS. Landed well with show-only viewers. Audiences particularly like his genuine affection for Tessarion set against Ormund's coldly instrumental view of dragons. Some book-reader complaints that he has been changed too much.
Alive. Took part in the Sheepstealer fight.
Positive, tied to goodwill toward Addam.
ALIVE but poisoned with nightshade by Alicent and collapsed at Harrenhal. There is NO on-screen death. His fate is the season’s biggest open question.

MIXED BUT HIGHLY ENGAGED. 'Mommy issues' has become the shorthand for S3 Aemond. The Alys material works for viewers as gothic psychological horror, not romance. There is real fatigue about another Targaryen stuck at Harrenhal hallucinating.
Alive. Appeared in E7 only inside Helaena's VISION — she has not flown into combat.
Big excitement at finally seeing her; a wave of explainers and edits since E7.
Alive and pregnant, effectively a Black ward/prisoner in King's Landing, still protecting Jaehaera.

INTENSELY PROTECTED. Generates unusually little hostility. Enormous excitement about Dreamfyre finally appearing, and viewers are decoding her visions rather than dismissing them. The instinct is 'protect Helaena at all costs'.
Alive, commanding Velaryon forces, and has just received proof of Corlys’s captivity.
WELL RECEIVED, especially his rage at the Gullet when Corlys appears to fall.
Alive.
Neutral to positive.
Alive with the Black river host. Known as Black Aly.
A POINT OF INTEREST since it emerged she personally shot Criston Cole.

contract.condition: The first candidate whom the episode definitively establishes as dead, ordered by the moment the death occurs or is first confirmed.
exclusions: A candidate already dead before the episode does not count.
An ambiguous disappearance, apparently fatal wound, or unconfirmed fall does not count.
Deaths of unnamed people and people outside the candidate list do not settle this prediction.

title_review.note: Named character means a listed candidate, and death requires definitive screen evidence or explicit confirmation.

contract.condition: The candidate with the greatest number of people or creatures they directly kill on screen during the episode; a shared highest total may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: Orders carried out by soldiers, allies, or a bonded dragon do not count as the candidate's direct kill.
Unconfirmed casualties and kills occurring wholly off screen do not count.
Damage, capture, and incapacitation without death do not count as kills.

title_review.note: On-screen kills is literal: the candidate must directly cause each visible death.

contract.condition: The candidate whom the operator judges to commit the episode's most consequential deliberate betrayal of an established ally, oath, or active agreement; an inseparable judgment may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: Open hostility, a previously declared change of side, or ordinary disagreement does not count as betrayal.
An accidental failure or coerced act without a meaningful choice does not count.
A suspected betrayal without an act or explicit confirmation does not count.

title_review.note: Biggest is an operator judgment about consequence, limited to deliberate betrayals shown or explicitly confirmed in the episode.

contract.condition: The candidate whose bonded or commanded dragon is first definitively killed or rendered unable to continue fighting during the episode.
exclusions: A dragon merely landing, retreating, being briefly grounded, or taking a non-disabling wound does not count.
A dragon's prior condition at the start of the episode does not count as falling in this episode.
A rider being separated from an otherwise capable dragon does not count.

title_review.note: Falls means the candidate's dragon is killed or clearly disabled from the fight, not merely knocked downward.

contract.condition: The candidate who is the primary subject of the episode's final unresolved revelation, reversal, or imminent threat immediately before the end credits.
exclusions: A candidate's presence in the final sequence does not count if another candidate is clearly the unresolved subject.
A resolved final beat, recap image, or credits image does not count as the cliffhanger.
General suspense about a battle or faction does not settle a candidate unless the final turn centers that candidate.

title_review.note: Centers on identifies the primary subject of the final unresolved story turn, not simply the last face shown.

contract.condition: The candidate whose side achieves the clearest tactical victory in the episode's principal organized battle; if the battle has two inseparable victors, they may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: A minor skirmish, duel, raid, or political exchange does not replace the episode's principal organized battle.
Strategic advantage without a clear battlefield result does not count as winning the battle.
If the principal battle remains unresolved, the prediction is void rather than awarded for momentum.

title_review.note: Wins refers to the episode's principal organized battle and allows a leader to receive the result achieved by their forces unless the episode refutes that command relationship.

contract.condition: The candidate visible latest in the episode's story footage before the end credits; candidates visible together in the final shot may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: Recap footage, opening-title imagery, end-credit art, and next-episode material do not count.
A name spoken after the candidate's last appearance does not make that candidate last on screen.
An indistinguishable distant figure does not count without a clear identity.

title_review.note: On screen means visibly identifiable in story footage immediately before credits.

contract.condition: The candidate with the greatest cumulative time visibly present in the episode's story footage; a measurement tie may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: Recap footage, opening titles, credits, and next-episode material do not count.
A scene discussing a candidate while they are absent does not count toward that candidate.
Voice-only presence does not count as screen time.

title_review.note: Screen time is cumulative visible presence in story footage, measured across the whole episode.

contract.condition: The first candidate to directly cause a fresh visible physical injury or death during the episode.
exclusions: Threats, property damage, restraint, and blows that cause no visible injury do not count.
An injury caused by the candidate's soldiers, allies, or dragon does not count for the candidate.
An injury that occurred before the episode or wholly off screen does not count.

title_review.note: First blood means the first directly caused visible injury or death, not the first hostile act.

contract.condition: The candidate who physically sits on the Iron Throne in the episode's present-day story.
exclusions: Standing beside, touching, approaching, or being proclaimed ruler near the throne does not count.
Dreams, visions, recaps, statues, and remembered earlier scenes do not count.
Sitting on another throne or ceremonial chair does not count.

title_review.note: Sits is literal and the object must be the Iron Throne in present-day story action.

contract.condition: The candidate whom the operator judges to end the episode with the most severe net combination of danger, loss, captivity, injury, isolation, or loss of power; an inseparable judgment may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: A candidate's pre-existing hardship does not count unless the episode materially worsens it.
Temporary embarrassment or a setback already reversed by episode end does not outweigh lasting consequences.
Speculative future danger unsupported by the final state does not count.

title_review.note: Worst position is an operator comparison of each candidate's net end-of-episode state, not a single objective metric.

contract.condition: The candidate who newly establishes an accepted rider bond with, or clear rider control over, an unclaimed dragon during the episode.
exclusions: Approaching, touching, feeding, surviving, or speaking to a dragon without accepted control does not count.
Continuing or restoring a bond that existed before the episode does not count as claiming a dragon.
Commanding a dragon through another rider does not count.

title_review.note: Claims means a new accepted rider bond or clear rider control, not mere contact with a dragon.

contract.condition: The first candidate shown riding a dragon in sustained airborne travel or combat during the episode.
exclusions: Mounting a grounded dragon without visible flight does not count.
Recap footage, dreams, visions, and next-episode material do not count.
A candidate merely accompanying or commanding another rider does not count.

title_review.note: Ride requires visible sustained airborne travel or combat in the episode's story footage.

contract.condition: The first candidate audibly shown speaking the exact word 'Dracarys' in the episode's story footage.
exclusions: Recap audio, opening or credit audio, next-episode material, and an unidentifiable voice do not count.
A subtitle, written word, or another character quoting the candidate does not count.
A different High Valyrian command does not count.

title_review.note: Say is literal: the candidate's identifiable voice must speak the exact command in story footage.

contract.condition: The candidate whose sustained spoken address the operator judges strongest in performance, rhetoric, and consequence during the episode; an inseparable judgment may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: A single quip, brief command, ordinary conversation, or voiceover fragment does not count as a speech.
The importance of a scene without a sustained address does not make it a speech.
A speech only reported by another character does not count.

title_review.note: Best is an operator judgment among sustained spoken addresses, using performance, rhetoric, and consequence.

contract.condition: The candidate who survives a direct mortal threat that the episode presents as likely to kill them, with the operator selecting the clearest case; inseparable cases may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: General wartime danger, political precarity, or an old threat that does not become immediate in the episode does not count.
A candidate who avoids danger before it becomes a direct mortal threat does not count.
An unresolved apparent death does not count as survival.

title_review.note: Against all odds means surviving an immediate episode-presented mortal threat, with the clearest case chosen by the operator.

contract.condition: The first candidate whose identifiable voice speaks intelligible dialogue in the episode's story footage.
exclusions: Recap audio, opening narration outside the story, and next-episode material do not count.
Breathing, crying, grunts, screams, and other nonverbal sounds do not count as dialogue.
An unidentifiable off-screen voice does not count until its speaker is established.

title_review.note: Line of dialogue means the first intelligible spoken words by an identifiable candidate in story footage; the speaker need not be visible.

contract.condition: The first candidate visibly shown shedding tears or unmistakably sobbing during the episode's story footage.
exclusions: A sad expression, reddened eyes, or a breaking voice without visible tears or unmistakable sobbing does not count.
Recap footage, dreams, visions, and next-episode material do not count.
Another character reporting that the candidate cried does not count.

title_review.note: Cry requires visible tears or unmistakable sobbing in story footage.

contract.condition: The candidate whose sustained look the operator judges most clearly intimidating or threatening during the episode; an inseparable judgment may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: A neutral reaction shot, ordinary concentration, or a look whose target and menace are unclear does not count.
Threatening dialogue without a qualifying sustained look does not count.
Recap footage and promotional material do not count.

title_review.note: Most menacing is an operator judgment among sustained, clearly threatening looks shown in the episode.

contract.condition: The candidate whose spoken line the operator judges most foolish, absurd, or self-defeating in context during the episode; an inseparable judgment may be settled as a tie.
exclusions: A bad decision without a qualifying spoken line does not count.
A line made wrong only by information unavailable to the speaker does not count unless it is also foolish in context.
A quotation reported by another character does not count as the candidate saying it.

title_review.note: Dumbest is an operator judgment about a candidate's own spoken line in its scene context.

commentary_voices.name: Ned
commentary_voices.instruction: State the record plainly, with grave restraint and no ornamental judgment.

commentary_voices.name: Cersei
commentary_voices.instruction: Judge power with clipped contempt, political precision, and no self-doubt.

commentary_voices.name: Tyrion
commentary_voices.instruction: Use dry intelligence to expose the strategic contradiction without trivializing its human cost.

commentary_voices.name: Joffrey
commentary_voices.instruction: Mistake cruelty for strength with loud certainty and revealingly poor judgment.

commentary_voices.name: Daenerys
commentary_voices.instruction: Speak with sincere conviction, direct moral stakes, and no ironic retreat.

commentary_voices.name: Olenna
commentary_voices.instruction: Deliver one economical, amused verdict whose final clause carries the blade.

commentary_voices.name: Arya
commentary_voices.instruction: Use few words, attend to cowardice and earned consequence, and land the judgment cleanly.

commentary_requests.speaker: ned
commentary_requests.angle: Acknowledge why the audience protects Sheepstealer while keeping the witnessed wound and isolation central.

commentary_requests.speaker: cersei
commentary_requests.angle: Treat the audience's deteriorating confidence as a judgment on how power is being used, not proof of an unwitnessed downfall.

commentary_requests.speaker: tyrion
commentary_requests.angle: Complicate the betrayal by recognizing that viewers understand Ulf's grievance without excusing what he has done.

commentary_requests.speaker: joffrey
commentary_requests.angle: Admire Ormund's control for the wrong reasons while staying inside the witnessed prisoner, alliance, and approaching-army facts.

commentary_requests.speaker: daenerys
commentary_requests.angle: Play the scarred king and dragon reunion sincerely, without inventing how Sunfyre survived or what happens next.

commentary_requests.speaker: olenna
commentary_requests.angle: Separate criticism of Alicent's written choice from respect for the performance, then end on the political cost of her bargain.

commentary_requests.speaker: arya
commentary_requests.angle: Recognize the audience's interest in Black Aly through the one witnessed fact they are responding to, without adding another kill.
